name: PgQue
summary: Skype’s PgQ engine repackaged as one SQL file: a zero-bloat event log inside any Postgres 14+.
intro: PgQue is a queue written only in SQL and PL/pgSQL, installed from one file into any Postgres 14 or newer, managed services included. Producers call `pgque.send`, which appends an event to the queue’s table. A ticker records ticks, each storing a snapshot of which transactions had committed; by default `pg_cron` runs it in a one-second slot that ticks every 100 ms, and `pg_timetable` or your own scheduler also work. A batch is every event whose transaction committed between two ticks, found by comparing the two snapshots, so no rows are locked. Each consumer subscribes and keeps its own cursor: `receive` returns its next batch and `ack` moves the cursor on. Several consumers each see every event, more like a Kafka topic than a work queue; experimental cooperative consumers split one consumer’s batches across a pool of workers.

Most Postgres queues update or delete each row after use, leaving dead tuples for VACUUM, which can’t remove them while a long transaction or a stalled replica holds the xmin horizon. PgQue never deletes rows on its hot path. Each queue is three child tables; the ticker writes into one at a time and, once every consumer has read past the oldest, empties it with `TRUNCATE`, which frees the storage at once and leaves nothing to vacuum. The cost is latency: about 52 ms median from send to receive at the default tick. It’s free under Apache 2.0, and very new: the repository was created in April 2026 and the latest release is 0.2.2.
strengths: No dead tuples in the event tables, even with the xmin horizon pinned: in the project’s benchmark a `SKIP LOCKED` queue’s dead tuples grew about 14 times and its throughput fell 35%, while PgQue stayed at zero
Native fan-out: any number of consumers read the same log at their own pace without copying events
Pure SQL: no C extension, no `shared_preload_libraries` and no daemon, so it installs on RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Supabase and Neon
Retries with `nack`, a dead-letter queue, and separate reader, writer and admin roles come in the default install
The engine underneath, PgQ, has run in production since Skype built it in 2006, with hundreds of queues there by 2009
limits: Very new: created in April 2026 and still 0.x; its own README calls the API layer early-stage and marks cooperative consumers experimental
Nothing is delivered without a running ticker; with `pg_cron` it holds a background worker for each one-second slot, and `cron.job_run_details` grows until you purge it
Batching adds latency (about 52 ms median at 10 ticks a second), and send, tick and receive must be separate transactions; not for single-digit-millisecond dispatch
A stopped or slow consumer blocks table rotation, so the event tables keep growing until it catches up
No per-job priorities, scheduled delivery (`send_at`) or message TTL yet; for those, the project points to a job-queue framework

snippet.title: Two consumers on one queue, each receiving every event
source: -- install once, from a clone of the repo: \i sql/pgque.sql
select pgque.start();                         -- pg_cron ticker, 10 ticks a second
select pgque.subscribe('orders', 'emails');   -- also sees every event
-- in a later transaction, after the next tick
select pgque.ack(1);                          -- the batch_id from those rows

sections.title: pgmq, PgQue and PgQueuer
sections.intro: All three keep queues in Postgres tables. They differ in what a reader gets, which languages can join in, and how old rows are cleaned up.

rows.label: Model
values: Message queue: each message goes to one reader
Shared event log: every subscribed consumer sees every event
Job queue: Python workers run a handler per job

rows.label: What you install
values: SQL objects, as an extension or a plain SQL file
One PL/pgSQL file, plus a scheduler that calls the ticker
A Python package; `pgq install` creates its tables

rows.label: Languages
values: Any, through SQL; official Rust and Python clients
Any, through SQL; first-party Python, Go and TypeScript clients
Python 3.10+, async handlers

rows.label: Handing out work
values: `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, then a visibility timeout
Batches between ticks, found by comparing two transaction snapshots; no row locks
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, then status `picked` with a heartbeat

rows.label: Delivery
values: Exactly once within the visibility timeout, then at least once
At least once, in batches; about 52 ms median wait at the default 100 ms tick
At least once; handlers must be idempotent

rows.label: Retries
values: The message reappears after the timeout; track `read_ct` yourself
`nack` schedules a retry; a dead-letter queue after the limit
`RetryRequested` with a delay, or hold failed jobs for review

rows.label: Finished messages
values: Deleted, or moved to an archive table
Stay in the log; `ack` moves the consumer’s cursor
Deleted from the queue; the outcome is appended to a log table

rows.label: Dead rows and cleanup
values: Updates and deletes leave dead rows for VACUUM; optional partitions dropped by pg_partman
None on the hot path: three tables rotate and the oldest is emptied with `TRUNCATE`
Deletes leave dead rows; `pgq autovac` makes autovacuum aggressive

notes: PgQue’s latency figure comes from its own committed benchmark.

story: In 2006 Skype needed asynchronous processing and replication across its many Postgres databases. Marko Kreen built PgQ, a queue inside Postgres that reused the snapshot-based event handling of the Slony-I replication system. Its first user was Londiste, Skype’s replication tool. Skype open-sourced PgQ in 2007 as part of SkyTools, and by 2009 it ran hundreds of queues and consumers there. Events were served in batches between ticks made by a separate ticker, and the queue’s three tables were rotated rather than deleted from.

PgQ needed a C extension and the `pgqd` daemon, which managed services such as RDS and Cloud SQL don’t allow. Meanwhile most newer Postgres queues claimed rows with `SKIP LOCKED` and deleted them when done, and write-ups such as Brandur’s 2015 post about Que at Heroku showed backlogs building as dead tuples outran VACUUM.

In April 2026 Nikolay Samokhvalov, founder of Postgres.ai and co-host of Postgres.fm, released PgQue 0.1. It keeps the PgQ engine and builds on PgQ’s pure PL/pgSQL path, with `pg_cron` replacing `pgqd`, 64-bit transaction ids, and a `send`, `receive` and `ack` API on top. Version 0.2 in May added first-party clients and sub-second ticks.

choices.choice: Batches from two snapshots, not row locks
choices.why: Whether an event belongs to a batch depends only on transaction visibility between two ticks, so delivery needs no row locks or per-row deletes, and every consumer can run the same test against its own cursor.

choices.choice: Rotate three tables and `TRUNCATE` the oldest
choices.why: `TRUNCATE` drops a table’s storage at once with no dead tuples. Table inheritance is used rather than declarative partitioning because a cheap truncate-and-reuse cycle per table is exactly what rotation needs.
Managed Postgres won’t load C extensions or run a custom daemon beside the database, but `pg_cron` is available on the major providers.

choices.choice: Keep the engine, change the surface
choices.why: PgQ’s batch, tick, rotation and consumer-tracking core had a decade of production use, so PgQue leaves it unchanged and only modernizes types and adds a friendlier API and roles.

timeline.text: Marko Kreen starts PgQ at Skype, inspired by Slony-I
Open-sourced in SkyTools; Londiste replication is its first user
SkyTools 3 alpha adds cascading, cooperative consumers and the `pgqd` daemon
PgQue 0.1 ships in April as a single SQL file
0.2 adds Python, Go and TypeScript clients and sub-second ticks
